title: Plug in a trailer's 7-way connector under its spring cover
instruction: Plug the black 7-way plug fully into the trailer's socket so that the socket's cover closes down behind the plug's latch ear, then let go of it.
context: Coupling a tractor to a trailer includes plugging in the 7-way electrical line that powers the trailer's lights and brakes: the driver holds the socket's spring cover up, pushes the plug fully home and lets the cover latch it, or the plug can work loose on the road. O*NET lists connecting air or electrical lines when coupling trailers as a task of heavy and tractor-trailer truck drivers (53-3032.00, about 2.2 million workers).
setup: A table in front of two arms (bases 61 cm apart), seen by one overhead camera and a camera on each wrist. Distances are measured forward from the line between the arm bases and sideways from the midpoint between them. (1) A trailer's front wall: a white-painted steel panel, 40 x 42 cm and 3 mm thick, standing upright crosswise on the table, its front face 33.8 cm forward, centred on the centre line, with a red stripe along its top. (2) A grey die-cast SAE J560-style 7-way socket mounted on the wall: flange 9.6 x 6.2 cm with two screws; its round mouth faces the arms, centred on the centre line 19 cm above the table, the mouth's face 33 cm forward; bore 41 mm across and 45 mm deep to the contact insert, with a 10 mm keyway on its left and a chamfered rim. Its grey cover, 6 cm wide and 3.4 cm long, hangs shut over the mouth from a hinge 3.3 cm above the bore's centre, held shut by its spring; it has a 7 mm latch lip along the inside of its free edge and a 12 mm thumb lip along the outside, and opens up to 125 degrees. (3) A black SAE J560-style 7-way plug, 12.3 cm long, 180 g: a 38.5 mm barrel 5.9 cm long with a key rib on its left side and a yellow band painted around it 4.5 cm back from its face; behind the barrel a latch ear on top (ramped at its front) and one underneath, 5.8 cm across the pair; then a 4.2 cm body and a cord grommet. It is parked in a black keyed parking cup (41 mm inside, 3.3 cm deep) on a post: the cup's mouth 30 cm forward and 17 cm right of the centre line, the plug's axis level, 19 cm above the table, pointing forward, its face 3 cm inside the cup. (4) Its cord: a black 7-conductor cable, 1.4 cm thick, 55 cm long, 200 g, from the plug's back end down to the table, lying in an S to the right and fixed 3 cm above the table to a 2.4 x 2.4 cm post 20 cm forward and 30 cm right. The layout is the same in every trial, as in the screenshot.
scoring: 1.0 as soon as all of these hold, with the plug and cover still, for 1 s: the plug fully home (its face within 1.5 mm of the socket's contact insert, which hides the yellow band inside the socket's rim; its axis within 2 mm and 4 degrees of the socket's); the cover down on the plug with its latch lip behind the plug's top latch ear (the lip at least 2 mm below the top of the ear); and each gripper's fingertip centre at least 3 cm from the middle of the plug's body and from the middle of the cover's free edge. Otherwise, judged at the end of the run: 0.75: the same, but a gripper closer than 3 cm; 0.5: the plug fully home but the cover's lip not behind the ear; 0.25: the plug's face 1 cm or more inside the socket and within 4 mm of its axis, but not fully home; 0.0: anything else.
reset_notes: Nothing is consumed: hold the cover up, pull the plug out, park it in its cup with its key rib in the cup's keyway (on the left), and lay the cord back in its S as in the screenshot.
fidelity: Rigid-body simulation (Isaac Sim 6.1 with PhysX, 20 Hz control) of a calibrated two-arm table. Simplified: the socket and plug are built from boxes and cylinders, the seven electrical contacts are not modelled (the plug slides freely to its stop against the contact insert), the cover's spring is a spring in its hinge, the cord is a chain of 11 rigid segments, friction and contact use the simulator's defaults, and the cameras render at 320 x 176.
